en: The *rāvaṇabaddha* meter consists of the following:
the first quarter has eight syllables, the second has twelve, the third has eight, and the fourth has twelve;
the final syllable of each quarter is heavy (*guru*), and the first syllable of each quarter is light (*laghu*). This is known as the *śliṣṭāvasānaka* (rhymed-ending) meter.

The *sāṃhita* (euphonic combination), the *ṣoṇa*, and the *sāṃhita*; [the former] occurs at the junction (*saṃdhi*) where a vowel follows a word-final *ṛ*, and [the latter] occurs when a word-final *u*, *ū*, or visarga follows a word-final *i* or *ī*. These sixteen [types of *sāṃhita*] are respectively designated as sixteen distinct *gaṇas* (classes) within their own respective categories.
At the beginning, there should be three groups of two syllables each;
then the fourth is said to consist of one, and the fifth of two;
then the sixth group consists of three, and the seventh likewise consists of three.
If there is one [short syllable], it would be the eighth; thus, eight groups (gaṇas) are traditionally taught.
At the beginning of the seven [groups], there is that which indicates the uneven and even numbers, while here for the eighth group, it shall be the indicator of the number.
Up to fifty syllables, each one is proclaimed in succession;
sometimes with four, five, six, three, seven,
eight, nine, or ten syllables.
And in this way, each individual statement is characterized by six vowels;

in this [system], *ra* and so on, *la*, *ka*, and *ṭa* are the things to be numbered, starting from the beginning in sequence. Furthermore, there are five distinct groups beginning with *ra* and *sa*, and therein the number shall be determined again.

The eight vowels (*svara*) are, in order: *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*, *e*, *o*, and *ai*; [the others] are not to be observed here. The consonants (*hal*) are *da*, *ja*, *ba*, *ma*, *na*, *ka*, *ḍa*, *ga*, *ya*, *ra*, and *va*; the eleventh is *la*.
However, other [consonants] such as *ra*, *sa*, *ḍa*, etc., are not to be observed here; thus, in this context, there are only vowels (*ac*) and consonants (*hal*).
One should avoid those places where the colors (or syllables) are indistinct;
first,
having combined each respective group according to its uniform nature through the calculation of the *vigaṇas*.

The number of those [syllables] should be understood as equal or unequal in each respective case. If the first and third [feet] begin with *ja* and *i*, the odd [feet] are known as "Viṣama"; if they begin with *ga* and *sa*, the odd [feet] are "Samagaṇa";
if they begin with *u* and *ma*, the second [foot] is "Viṣama"; and if they begin with *ba* and *a*, it is remembered as "Sama. 13.

If the third [foot] is even, it should be even; if it were odd, it would be odd. These three groups here—if the odd [feet] are *uga*, then it is odd; if they are *uḍa*, then it is even here—this is certain.
Among these, when two groups (gaṇas) consist of one long syllable each, they may be either even or uneven;
the other [groups] would be the opposite of that.
For the first, second, and so on, up to the eighth, the preceding and following syllables occur in sequence. 15–16.

In this case, if the fourth *gaṇa* consists of two or eight *mātrās*, it indicates an irregularity (*asama*), whereas for the fifth *gaṇa*, if it consists of two or eight *mātrās*, a regularity (*sama*) is observed; likewise, if it consists of five *mātrās*, it is considered irregular (*vaiṣamya*). Furthermore, if the [fifth] *gaṇa* consists of five *mātrās*, it is likewise considered regular (*sama*).

If the sixth gaṇa here is *va*, there is inequality; if it is not *va*, it is equal. (18) Here, for the seventh gaṇa, it would be equal if it belongs to the first five [groups] beginning with *ra*; it is easily understood that the seventh is unequal if it belongs to the first five [groups] beginning with *sa*. (19)
Having discarded the five groups of five [syllables] here that are devoid of the *visarga* and lacking the *gaṇas*, one should determine the count—
namely one, two, three, four, or five— by means of the six [tastes] (*rasa*) and so forth during the final calculation of the *gaṇas*.
If words such as *rāda* and others were to indicate the absence of *visarga*, then the term "akhaṇḍamārgapada" would not be perceived here;
furthermore, in this context, there would be prefixes (*upasargas*) such as *atretyanta* and *paretyeti*. 21–22.
Indeed, they are not to be counted here among the characteristics at the end of words,
nor are they to be reckoned here in the enumerations of long vowels; likewise,
wherever there is an absence of a *lakṣya*, in each such case it is traditionally held to be equal [to its predecessor].
In the Yajurveda, one should always perform the *unnayana* (the lifting up) in this very manner for fifty [verses].
Thus ends the *Rāvaṇabhaiṭparibhāṣā*.
